claim: The timeout timer callback is operationally blind: sets timedOut and destroys the stream with no telemetry/logging, and .catch(()=>{}) swallows every destroy/reader.cancel rejection.
raw: The timeout timer callback is **operationally blind**: it sets `timedOut` and calls `void stream.destroy().catch(() => {})` with **no telemetry and no logging** — `fetcherService.ts:344-346`. ... the `.catch(() => {})` swallows every rejection from `destroy()`/`reader.cancel()`

claim: SSE_FIRST_CHUNK_TIMEOUT_MS (120s) and SSE_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS (60s) are hard-coded compile-time constants with no experiment-config backing and no kill switch, diverging from the getExperimentBasedConfig/ConfigKey convention in this path.
raw: `SSE_FIRST_CHUNK_TIMEOUT_MS` (120s) and `SSE_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS` (60s) are **hard-coded compile-time constants with no experiment-config backing and no kill switch** — `fetcherService.ts:303,310`. This diverges from the established convention (`getExperimentBasedConfig`/`ConfigKey`).

claim: StreamIdleTimeoutError is under-specified and orphaned — no .code/retryable classification, never used in retry/error-classification (canRetryOnceNetworkError never retries it), and timeoutMs/isFirstChunk live only in the message string.
raw: `StreamIdleTimeoutError` is **under-specified and orphaned** ... **never in any retry/error-classification code** ... `canRetryOnceNetworkError` ... never retries it ... the constructor's `timeoutMs`/`isFirstChunk` args are baked only into the message string (no fields)

claim: The idle timer is per-chunk resettable with no absolute stream-duration cap and no minimum-throughput check — a slow byte-drip holds the connection open indefinitely and grows SSEProcessor.extraData unbounded.
raw: The idle timer is **per-chunk resettable with no absolute stream-duration cap and no minimum-throughput check** — `fetcherService.ts:354`. A malicious ... upstream ... can send one byte ... just under every 60s to hold the connection open **indefinitely** ... grows `extraData` unbounded

claim: No test exercises a chunk arriving at/near the exact idle-timeout deadline (the chunk-vs-timer boundary); all 'does not time out' cases push chunks with a 100ms safety margin.
raw: **No test exercises a chunk arriving at/near the exact idle-timeout deadline** (the chunk-vs-timer boundary) — `streamIdleTimeout.spec.ts:342` (all "does not time out" cases push chunks with a 100ms safety margin).

raw: The **inline-completions SSE loop was left unwrapped** — `extensions/copilot/src/extension/completions-core/vscode-node/lib/src/openai/stream.ts:293` iterates a `DestroyableStream` with the identical `for await (const chunk of this.body)` shape but was not given `withStreamIdleTimeout`

claim: The JSDoc for SSE_FIRST_CHUNK_TIMEOUT_MS says it gives 'slightly more time' than the idle timeout, but 120000ms vs 60000ms is exactly 2x (an extra full minute).
raw: The JSDoc for `SSE_FIRST_CHUNK_TIMEOUT_MS` says it gives "slightly more time" than the idle timeout — `fetcherService.ts:301`. Verified values: 120000ms vs 60000ms — it is exactly **2× (an extra full minute)**, not a marginal increase.

claim: No test exercises a chunk arriving at/near the exact idle-timeout deadline (chunk-vs-timer race); a boundary probe produced an 'Invalid state: Controller is already closed' unhandled rejection.
raw: No test exercises a chunk arriving at/near the exact idle-timeout deadline (the 'race between chunk and timer' case). All 'does not time out' tests in streamIdleTimeout.spec.ts push chunks with a 100ms safety margin before the deadline (e.g. lines 111-115, 133-135) — none probe the boundary itself.

claim: The withStreamIdleTimeout(response.body) call site inside processResponseFromMessagesEndpoint has zero test coverage of any kind.
raw: The withStreamIdleTimeout(response.body) call site inside processResponseFromMessagesEndpoint has zero test coverage of any kind. Verified: `grep -rn "processResponseFromMessagesEndpoint" extensions/copilot/src` only shows the definition (messagesApi.ts:543) and its call from chatEndpoint.ts:372

claim: Neither timeout test asserts that stream.destroy()/reader.cancel() was actually invoked; the only evidence is indirect (the pending read resolving).
raw: Neither timeout test ('throws ... when first chunk never arrives', lines 55-72, or 'throws ... when a subsequent chunk stalls', lines 74-97) asserts that stream.destroy()/reader.cancel() was actually invoked. The only evidence is indirect

claim: Behavior when the underlying iterator.next() rejects (a real network/parse error, not a timeout) is completely untested — the not-masquerading-as-timeout contract has zero regression coverage.
raw: Behavior when the underlying iterator.next() rejects (a real network/parse error, not a timeout) is completely untested. ... the rejection to propagate as-is through the try/finally ... correctly NOT masquerading as a StreamIdleTimeoutError — but this contract has zero regression coverage.

claim: No test covers an empty stream (closed with zero chunks pushed); a regression treating 'closed with no data' as a first-chunk timeout would not be caught.
raw: No test covers an empty stream (closed with zero chunks pushed). ... Current behavior is correct (yields [], does not throw), but this is untested — a regression that treated 'stream closed with no data' as a first-chunk timeout (or vice versa) would not be caught.

claim: The error matchers in both timeout tests check only err.name and a message substring, never err instanceof StreamIdleTimeoutError, so a look-alike error would still pass.
raw: The error matchers in both timeout tests (lines 66-70 and 91-95) check only `err.name === 'StreamIdleTimeoutError'` and a message substring, never `err instanceof StreamIdleTimeoutError`.

claim: Only two of three call sites are exercised, and only on the fast/normal path (synchronous chunks, real timers); no test confirms a mid-stream StreamIdleTimeoutError propagates sensibly through the call sites.
raw: Of the 3 production call sites, only responsesApi.ts:537 ... and stream.ts:323 ... are exercised at all, and both only cover the fast/normal path — createFakeStreamResponse delivers all chunks synchronously with real (non-fake) timers, so the timeout branch is never triggered

claim: If stream.destroy() causes the pending iterator.next() to reject instead of resolving {done:true}, the typed StreamIdleTimeoutError is never thrown — the raw destroy error propagates, bypassing the if(timedOut) check.
raw: StreamIdleTimeoutError is only surfaced if timing out causes the wrapped iterator to resolve with `{done: true}`; if `stream.destroy()` instead causes the pending `iterator.next()` promise to *reject*, the descriptive timeout error is never thrown ... bypassing the `if (timedOut)` check

claim: StreamIdleTimeoutError constructor receives timeoutMs and isFirstChunk but never stores them as instance properties, only using them to build the message string.
raw: StreamIdleTimeoutError constructor receives timeoutMs and isFirstChunk but never stores them as instance properties, only using them to build the message string.

claim: The timeout-triggered destroy is fully swallowed: void stream.destroy().catch(() => {}) discards any error from destroy() with no logging.
raw: The timeout-triggered destroy is fully swallowed: `void stream.destroy().catch(() => { });` discards any error from `destroy()` with no logging. ... If the underlying stream's `destroy()` itself fails ... there is no signal anywhere in this code path that cleanup didn't succeed

claim: StreamIdleTimeoutError bakes timeoutMs and isFirstChunk only into the message string with no fields; the PR's own tests must use message.includes(...) to distinguish timeout kinds — a stringly-typed invariant.
raw: StreamIdleTimeoutError (lines 312-318) bakes timeoutMs and isFirstChunk only into the formatted `message` string; it has no `timeoutMs`/`isFirstChunk` fields ... The PR's own test ... has to do `err.message.includes('first chunk')` / `.includes('inactivity')` to tell the two timeout kinds apart

claim: void stream.destroy().catch(() => {}) swallows every rejection from stream.destroy()/reader.cancel() with zero logging/context; a systematic destroy failure (and the cancel-path telemetry) vanishes, making the feature undiagnosable.
raw: In the timeout callback of withStreamIdleTimeout, `void stream.destroy().catch(() => { });` swallows every possible rejection from stream.destroy() (i.e. ReadableStreamDefaultReader.cancel()) with zero logging and zero context. This is a maximally broad catch-all

claim: processSSE's finally unconditionally calls await this.cancel() -> this.response.body.destroy() unguarded; if that destroy() rejects, a throw from the finally replaces and masks the in-flight StreamIdleTimeoutError.
raw: The finally block at line 303 unconditionally calls `await this.cancel()`, which does `await this.response.body.destroy();` with no try/catch. If that destroy() rejects, a throw from inside a finally block replaces any exception already propagating — silently discarding the StreamIdleTimeoutError

claim: createControllableStream builds a ReadableStream with no custom cancel algorithm, so destroy() always resolves in tests; the destroy()/reader.cancel()-rejecting case during the timeout handler is unverified.
raw: createControllableStream builds a ReadableStream with no custom `cancel` algorithm, so `stream.destroy()` always resolves successfully in every test in this file. None of the new tests exercise the case ... destroy()/reader.cancel() rejecting during the timeout handler (fetcherService.ts:346)

claim: JSDoc for SSE_FIRST_CHUNK_TIMEOUT_MS says the first-chunk timeout gives 'slightly more time', but 120000ms is exactly double the 60000ms idle timeout (100% more, +60s).
raw: JSDoc for SSE_FIRST_CHUNK_TIMEOUT_MS says the first-chunk timeout gives the model 'slightly more time' than SSE_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS. Verified values: SSE_FIRST_CHUNK_TIMEOUT_MS = 2*60*1000 = 120000ms ... The first-chunk timeout is exactly double (100% more, +60s), not a marginal/'slight' increase.

claim: The withStreamIdleTimeout JSDoc doesn't note that the destroy() call is fire-and-forget with swallowed errors, so a destroy() failure is silently discarded and only the StreamIdleTimeoutError surfaces.
raw: the doc doesn't note that the destroy() call is fire-and-forget with swallowed errors (line 346: `void stream.destroy().catch(() => {})`) — if destroy() itself fails, that failure is silently discarded and only the StreamIdleTimeoutError surfaces.

claim: The watchdog destroys the stream and throws StreamIdleTimeoutError with no telemetry or logging; not being AbortError, it lands in generic error-outcome telemetry, so timeout frequency and false-positive rate cannot be measured after rollout.
raw: The idle/first-chunk watchdog destroys the stream and throws StreamIdleTimeoutError with no telemetry or logging. Because the error name is not 'AbortError', isAbortError() is false and it lands in generic error-outcome telemetry, indistinguishable from other stream errors.

claim: SSE_FIRST_CHUNK_TIMEOUT_MS (120s) and SSE_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS (60s) are hardcoded constants with no experimentation-service backing or kill switch; 60s is aggressive for reasoning models/long tool calls and gates all chat/agent/Anthropic streaming.
raw: SSE_FIRST_CHUNK_TIMEOUT_MS (120s) and SSE_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS (60s) are hardcoded compile-time constants with no experimentation-service backing or kill switch, unlike other tunables in this codebase (getExperimentBasedConfig/ConfigKey). A 60s idle limit is aggressive for reasoning models

claim: StreamIdleTimeoutError is orphaned — referenced only at definition/throw/wrap sites/tests, never in error-handling; canRetryOnceNetworkError never retries it and its raw developer message flows to generic error rendering.
raw: StreamIdleTimeoutError is orphaned: it is referenced only at its definition, throw, the three wrap sites, and tests, never in error-handling code. It is thrown mid-stream after the fetch resolved, so canRetryOnceNetworkError (which only guards the initial fetch) never retries it

claim: The inline-completions SSE loop iterates a DestroyableStream with the identical pattern but was left unwrapped by withStreamIdleTimeout, so the ghost-text/completions path remains vulnerable to the same hung-stream condition.
raw: The inline-completions SSE loop iterates a DestroyableStream with the identical pattern as the three wrapped call sites but was left unwrapped by withStreamIdleTimeout, so the ghost-text/completions path remains vulnerable to the exact hung-stream condition this PR fixes.

claim: withStreamIdleTimeout uses a per-chunk resettable idle timer with no absolute cap or minimum-throughput check; a slow-drip endpoint (1 byte or ':' keep-alive per <60s) holds the connection open indefinitely and grows extraData unbounded.
raw: withStreamIdleTimeout uses a per-chunk resettable idle timer with no absolute stream-duration cap or minimum-throughput check. A malicious/compromised/buggy model endpoint can drip one byte (or an ignored ':' SSE keep-alive comment) just under every 60s to hold the connection open indefinitely

claim: StreamIdleTimeoutError is a bare Error subclass with no classification metadata (no .code, not abort, no retryable flag); existing classifiers don't recognize it, so a hung-stream timeout becomes a hard, non-retryable, user-visible failure.
raw: StreamIdleTimeoutError is a bare Error subclass that carries no classification metadata (no `.code`, not an abort error, no retryable flag) and is referenced nowhere outside its definition and tests ... A hung-stream timeout matches none of these, so it falls through to generic fatal-error handling
